sets.q3: Intersection, union, difference: which part is which?
sets.q4: De Morgan: what is the opposite of an intersection?
sets.q5: How many go to at least one club? The sieve
sets.opsIntro: Two or three circles cut the universe into regions: each region says which circles you are inside and which you are outside. Pick an expression, or switch on free drawing, shade whatever you like, and see what the result is called.
sets.opsDef1: Union (A ∪ B): what lies in A or in B — one of them is enough.
sets.opsDef2: Intersection (A ∩ B): what lies in A and in B as well.
sets.opsDef3: Difference (A ∖ B): what lies in A but not in B.
sets.opsDef4: Complement (Ā): the part of the universal set that falls outside A.
sets.opsNoName: This shading has no simple name among the ones listed. Every set of regions can be described, but not all of them have a short form.
sets.opsElemNote: ⊆ stands between two sets, ∈ between an element and a set. The number 6 is an element of the set of even numbers (6 ∈ A), while the set of multiples of 6 is not an element of it but a subset (⊆), because every one of its elements lies in A.
sets.opsTask: Shade the region this expression denotes. Click the diagram or use the buttons.
sets.opsHint: Shade only what lies in A but in neither B nor C.
sets.dmIntro: "I have an umbrella and a cap." When is that false? Not only when you have neither — one of them missing is enough. Sets work the same way: the complement of A ∩ B is not Ā ∩ B̄. Switch between the two laws and compare the left and right drawings.
sets.dmAria_inter_left: Venn diagram: complement of A intersect B
sets.dmAria_inter_right: Venn diagram: union of the complements of A and B
sets.dmAria_union_left: Venn diagram: the complement of the union of A and B
sets.dmAria_union_right: Venn diagram: the intersection of the complement of A and the complement of B
sets.dmSame: The two shadings are identical: the left and the right side cover exactly the same regions.
sets.dmNote: De Morgan’s two laws: negating an intersection gives the union of the negations, and negating a union gives their intersection. So negation always swaps “and” for “or”, and the other way round.
sets.dmTask: Which expression describes the shaded region?
sets.dmHint: It is the shared part that is left out. That makes it the complement of the intersection.
sets.dmRegionsHint: The shading covers {{regions}} of the four regions.
sets.countIntro: In a class 18 go to football, 15 to swimming and 7 to both. Add 18 and 15 and you have counted those 7 people twice. Retype the region sizes, drag the slider and watch the × marks: when the sieve finishes, every region must read exactly ×1.
sets.countStep0: Start from nothing. Drag the slider right and the sieve builds up one step at a time.
sets.countStepMid: Look at the × marks: overlapping regions have now been counted more than once. The next step corrects that.
sets.countStepDone: Every region reads ×1. That is exactly why the sieve works: after the alternating sum, each element has been counted precisely once.
sets.countTask: A class has {{all}} students. Of them {{foot}} play football, {{swim}} swim, and {{both}} do both. How many do neither?
sets.countHint: First work out how many do at least one sport, then subtract from the class size.

logic.q1: What is the negation of “greater than 6”?
logic.q2: And, or, exclusive or: the mathematical “or” is not the one you think
logic.q4: If…, then…: when is it false, and what is its converse?
logic.negIntro: “The number is greater than 6.” What is its negation? Not “less than 6”: 6 itself is left out of the original, so the negation has to contain it. Negation is the complement — it selects exactly the elements the original left out. Pick a property and switch the negation on and off.
logic.negDef1: Statement: a declarative sentence that is unambiguously either true or false; those two options are its truth value.
logic.negDef2: Negation: the negation of a statement P (¬P, read "not P") is the statement that is true exactly when P is false.
logic.negSentence2: ¬¬P: it is not true that the element is not {{p}}, that is, the element is {{p}}.
logic.negPairsTitle: Common negations, and the common mistake
logic.negPair_and_s: It is raining and the wind is blowing.
logic.negPair_and_w: It is not raining and the wind is not blowing.
logic.negPair_and_r: It is not raining or the wind is not blowing.
logic.negPair_all_r: There is a student who did not bring their book.
logic.negPair_some_s: There is a number that is negative.
logic.negPair_some_w: There is a number that is not negative.
logic.negTask: What is the negation of "The number is greater than 6."? Pick one, then compare the two selections: the negation must select exactly the elements the original left out.
logic.negHint: The negation of "greater than 6" must include 6 itself, since 6 is not greater than 6.
logic.negChoiceNotGt7: The number is not greater than 7.
logic.negChoiceLt7: The number is less than 7 but not 6.
logic.negTaskOriginal: The original statement is true for these elements:
logic.connIntro: “Tea or coffee?” — everyday “or” means one of the two. The mathematical “or” is inclusive: both being true is fine as well. Pick two properties, switch between the three connectives, and see which elements the compound statement is true for.
logic.connSentence_xor: The element is either {{a}} or {{b}} (but not both).
logic.vennConnAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties A and B, the result of the connective shaded
logic.connRowHint: Each row of the table is one region of the diagram. Hover over a row!
logic.connOrNote: The mathematical “or” is inclusive: A ∨ B is true even when both are true. When everyday speech says “either…, or…”, that is the exclusive or: exactly one of the two.
logic.connTask: Select the elements that are either even or divisible by 3, in the exclusive sense!
logic.connHint: 6 and 12 are both even and divisible by 3. The exclusive or rules out exactly those.
logic.quantIntro: “Every element greater than 6 is even.” True? A single counterexample — 7, say — brings it down. “There is” works the other way round: one example confirms it. Build a statement and see what it turns into when you negate it.
logic.quantDef1: For all (∀): "every element …" is true when there is not a single exception. There is (∃): "there is an element that …" is true when at least one such element exists.
logic.quantDef2: Counterexample: a single case for which a "for all" statement fails. One counterexample brings the whole statement down.
logic.quantNoWitness: There is not a single example.
logic.quantNegSentence_all: Negation: There is an {{d}} that is not {{p}}. →
logic.quantNegNote: Notice that of the statement and its negation, exactly one is true. The negation of "every element is even" is not "no element is even" but "there is an element that is not even".
logic.quantTask: "Every element greater than 6 is even." This statement is false. Mark a counterexample!
logic.quantHint: A counterexample is an element that is greater than 6 but not even.
logic.impIntro: “If it rains, I take an umbrella.” That is a promise, and you can break it in only one way: it rains and you take no umbrella. If it does not rain, the promise holds whatever you do. Switch between the three modes and see which region can bring the statement down.
logic.impDef: Implication ("if P, then Q", P ⇒ Q): P is the premise, Q the conclusion. The statement is false only when P is true but Q is false; in every other case it is true.
logic.impConverseDef: Converse: the converse of “if P, then Q” is “if Q, then P”. It is a statement of its own, and its truth value may differ from the original’s.
logic.impSentence: If an element is {{p}}, then it is {{q}}. →
logic.impConverseSentence: Converse: If an element is {{q}}, then it is {{p}}. →
logic.iffSentence: An element is {{p}} if and only if it is {{q}}. →
logic.impCounter: Counterexample: {{list}}. For these the premise is true and the conclusion false.
logic.vennImpAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties P and Q, the refuting regions shaded
logic.impRowHint: The shaded regions are where the statement can fail. Hover over a row!
logic.impContraNote: Contrapositive: “if not Q, then not P” always says the same as the original “if P, then Q” — try it with any setting. That is why a statement can be proved by proving its contrapositive. The converse, on the other hand, is not the same: it is a separate statement with its own truth value.
logic.impTask: Given the statement "If a number is divisible by 6, then it is even." Pick its converse, then decide whether the converse is true or false!
logic.impHint: In the converse, premise and conclusion swap without negation. Then look for an even number that is not divisible by 6.
logic.impChoice_converse: If a number is even, then it is divisible by 6.
logic.impChoice_inverse: If a number is not divisible by 6, then it is not even.
logic.impChoice_contrapositive: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 6.

combi.q1: When do you multiply? The multiplication rule
combi.q2: When do you add, and when do you multiply?
combi.q3: How many orders, and what if two letters are the same?
combi.q4: Does the order matter? Team or podium
combi.q5: How many handshakes? Graphs and the complete graph
combi.q6: Can everyone know exactly three others?
combi.prodIntro: In the morning you pick one of 2 t-shirts and one of 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are there? Let us draw it. The first branching decides the t-shirt, the second the trousers, and the leaves of the tree are the finished outfits: 2 · 3 = 6.
combi.prodTreeAria: Choice tree with {{steps}} steps and {{total}} possibilities.
combi.prodTooMany: That is too many branches to draw: {{total}} possibilities. Remove a step or pick fewer options.
combi.prodLeaves: The number of leaves is the number of possibilities: {{total}}.
combi.prodRule: Multiplication rule: if a choice is made in several steps, and every step has the same number of options no matter what was chosen before, then the number of possibilities is the product of the options of the steps.
combi.prodTask: The canteen offers 3 soups, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different lunches can you put together if you take exactly one of each?
combi.prodHint: Three steps one after the other, and none of them affects the others: multiply.
combi.sumIntro: The snack bar has 4 sandwiches and 3 pastries. If you buy one thing, you have 4 + 3 = 7 choices: the two cases never mix, so we add them up. But if you buy a sandwich and a pastry, the two decisions come one after the other: 4 · 3 = 12. Switch between the two views and watch what changes in the picture.
combi.sumAria_or: {{a}} dots in the first row and {{b}} dots in the second, {{total}} dots in total.
combi.sumAria_and: A grid of dots with {{b}} rows and {{a}} columns, {{total}} dots in total.
combi.sumRead_or: You pick a single thing from one of the two groups: {{a}} + {{b}} = {{total}} possibilities.
combi.sumRead_and: You pick one from each group, and every dot is one pair: {{a}} · {{b}} = {{total}} possibilities.
combi.sumRule: Addition rule: if you split the possibilities into cases that exclude each other, you add up the sizes of the cases. This is case separation: you cut a hard problem into a few easier ones.
combi.wrongProblem: Problem: how many two-digit numbers can be made from the digits 1, 2, 3 if the two digits must be different?
combi.wrongStep1: The first digit can be chosen in 3 ways.
combi.wrongStep2: The second digit can also be chosen in 3 ways.
combi.wrongTask: One step of this solution is wrong. Which one?
combi.wrongHint: Write out all the numbers: 12, 13, 21, 23, 31, 32. Then check how many options are really left for the second place.
combi.wrongFix: The second digit can only be chosen in 2 ways, because the first digit cannot be used again. Correctly, 3 · 2 = {{total}} two-digit numbers can be made.
combi.orderIntro: A few friends line up for a photo. In how many orders can they stand? We count systematically: with three friends the first place has 3 options, the second the remaining 2, the third only 1, that is 3 · 2 · 1 = 6. This is the multiplication rule again, with one option fewer at every step. Change the number of friends!
combi.orderTreeAria: Tree of orders for {{n}} friends, with {{total}} orders.
combi.orderTooMany: {{total}} branches are too many to draw. The table shows how fast this number grows.
combi.orderResult: {{n}} friends can line up in {{total}} different orders: that is exactly how many leaves the tree has.
combi.orderDef: n factorial (n!): the product of the integers from 1 to n, n! = n · (n − 1) · … · 2 · 1. It is the number of ways n different things can be arranged in order. By convention 0! = 1.
combi.orderRule: n things can be arranged in order in n! ways. The number grows frighteningly fast: ten people can already line up in more than three million ways.
combi.orderWordIntro: Let us rearrange the letters of the word {{word}}. If we could tell the two A's apart there would be {{all}} orders. But we cannot, so every word would appear on the list exactly twice: {{all}} has to be divided by 2.
combi.orderTask: Five friends sit down on a bench. {{first}} and {{second}} insist on sitting next to each other. How many seatings are possible?
combi.orderHint: Glue the two of them into a single block: then only 4 things have to be arranged. Inside the block the two of them can still swap places.
combi.selIntro: We pick three of five classmates. If they form a team, the order we list them in makes no difference: Anna–Bence–Csilla is the same team as Csilla–Anna–Bence. But if they stand on the podium — gold, silver, bronze — a different order means a different medal. Switch between the two views and see how much the number grows.
combi.selDef: Variation (in English books: k-permutation): choosing k out of n things where the order matters. Combination: choosing k out of n things where the order does not matter. Every combination corresponds to k! variations.
combi.selPickPrompt: Pick {{k}} people above and we will show you the orders they can stand in.
combi.selResult_no: The order does not matter, so {{total}} different teams can be put together.
combi.selResult_yes: Every team of {{k}} can stand on the podium in {{each}} different orders, so counting the medals there are {{teams}} · {{each}} = {{total}} cases.
combi.selNames: Instead of memorising the names, always ask the question: does the order matter? If yes, it is a variation; if not, a combination.
combi.selLottoTitle: How big is this number really?
combi.selLottoYears: Years at one ticket a week
combi.selLottoNote: That is how many ways 5 numbers can be chosen out of 90. Filling in a single ticket a week, this is how many years it would take to try them all.
combi.selTask: A team of 3 is put together from a club of 8 people. How many different teams are possible?
combi.selHint: There is no order inside a team. First work out the ordered count, 8 · 7 · 6, then divide it by 3! = 6.
combi.graphIntro: Draw the people as dots, and join two of them when they shook hands. That is all a graph is: it does not matter where the dots sit or whether the lines are straight — only what is joined to what. Click two vertices one after the other (or use the buttons) and see how many edges it takes for everyone to shake hands with everyone.
combi.graphDef: Graph: a set of dots, the vertices, and lines joining some of them, the edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges that run into it.
combi.graphResult: There are {{edges}} edges drawn now. If everyone shook hands with everyone, {{complete}} edges would be needed — exactly the number of ways to choose two of the {{n}} vertices.
combi.graphCompleteNote: If everyone shakes hands with everyone, every pair of vertices gets exactly one edge. So an edge is nothing but a choice of two vertices without order — exactly what we counted in the previous section.
combi.graphTask: There are 7 people at a party and everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. How many handshakes are there?
combi.graphHint: Draw the complete graph on 7 vertices, or count like this: there are 7 · 6 handshake ends, but every handshake was counted twice.
combi.parityIntro: In a group everyone knows exactly three others. Is that possible with seven people? Add up the degrees: every acquaintance counts at two people, so the sum of the degrees can only be even. Set the head count and the degree, and see when such a graph can be drawn at all.
combi.parityPickD: How many others does everyone know?
combi.parityQuestion: Among {{n}} people everyone knows exactly {{d}} others. Is that possible?
combi.parityReason_ok: Yes, it is possible. The degrees would add up to {{sum}}, which means {{edges}} acquaintances, that is {{edges}} edges. One such graph is drawn below.
combi.parityReason_oddSum: Not possible. The degrees would add up to {{sum}}, which is odd — but the sum of the degrees is always twice the number of edges, so it is even.
combi.parityReason_degreeTooBig: Not possible. Nobody can know {{d}} others, because apart from themselves there are only {{n}} − 1 people.
combi.parityAria: Graph on {{n}} vertices where every vertex has degree {{d}}.
combi.parityNote: The sum of the degrees is always twice the number of edges, however you draw the graph. Every edge has two ends, and it adds one to the degree at each of them.
combi.parityTask: Can it happen that in a group of 9 people everyone knows exactly 3 others?
combi.parityHint: Multiply: 9 · 3 would be the sum of the degrees. But the sum of the degrees is always even.

num.q2: How does 0.2727… turn into a fraction?
num.q3: Where is √2 on the number line?
num.fracIntro: 0.2727… never ends, and yet a simple fraction is hiding behind it. The trick rests on one thing: multiplying by a power of ten only shifts the point, so after two shifts the two numbers have the very same endless tail, and subtracting wipes it out. Pick a decimal and follow the steps.
num.fracDef: Repeating decimal: a decimal in which a group of digits, the period, repeats for ever, for example 0.2727… The period is marked with a bar over it.
num.fracResult: The endless tail is gone: after the subtraction there is only a whole number left to divide, and the common fraction is ready.
num.fracTask: Write the number 0.363636… as a common fraction. Give the numerator and the denominator in lowest terms.
num.lineIntro: No fraction writes √2 down exactly, and yet it has one definite place on the number line — one you can find with a ruler and a pair of compasses. Stand a square of side 1 on the segment from 0 to 1: by Pythagoras its diagonal is √2 long, and all that is left is to lay that length onto the line.
num.lineSqrtAria: A unit square on the segment from 0 to 1, its diagonal swung onto the number line with an arc.
num.lineSqrtNote: No fraction writes this length down exactly, yet there it is on the line — a pair of compasses and a ruler find it. So irrational numbers are not something vague: they are points just as real as the rest.
num.lineZoomIntro: Pick a number and step further in. Each step cuts the interval into ten equal parts and asks which one the number falls into. The number of that part is exactly its next decimal digit.
num.lineZoomPickAria: Which number to zoom in on
num.lineZoomAria: The number line zoomed to {{level}} decimals, with {{name}} marked.
num.lineZoomNote_root2: The decimals of √2: {{digits}}… They never stop and never start repeating. That is the mark of an irrational number.
num.lineZoomNote_pi: The decimals of π: {{digits}}… Trillions of them have been worked out and nobody has found a pattern — nor will they, because π is irrational.
num.lineZoomNote_third: The decimals of 1/3: {{digits}}… The same 3 keeps coming. It is rational, and its period is a single digit long.
num.lineZoomNote_twentyTwoSevenths: The decimals of 22/7: {{digits}}… The block 142857 repeats for ever. This number is an old approximation of π, but it is not π: they part company at the third decimal.
num.lineTask: Which two neighbouring tenths does √10 fall between? Choose the lower one.
num.lineHint: Square them: 3.1² = 9.61, which is less than 10; 3.2² = 10.24, which is already more.

pow.q1: How many times can you fold a sheet of paper? Powers
pow.q2: Why is the zeroth power 1, and what does a negative exponent mean?
pow.q3: Why do the exponents add up? The laws as a picture
pow.q4: How do we write down the mass of the Earth? Normal form
pow.q5: What is a square root, and why is √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b?
pow.q6: What does a fractional exponent mean? x^(1/2) = √x
pow.defIntro: A sheet of paper is about 0.1 mm thick, and every fold doubles the number of layers. That is pure powering: 2ⁿ. First pick a base and an exponent to see how many factors the shorthand stands for — then drag the folding slider and watch where the paper gets to.
pow.defDef: Power: the notation aⁿ stands for the product of n factors, each equal to a. a is the base and n is the exponent. For example 2⁵ = 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 = 32: a product of five 2s.
pow.defFactorsAria: {{factors}} identical factors side by side, each of them {{base}}.
pow.defFoldIntro: Every fold doubles the number of layers, so the thickness is 0.1 mm · 2ⁿ. Drag the slider and watch how fast it runs away.
pow.defFoldStart: Nothing remarkable happens over the first few folds. Keep dragging.
pow.foldCmp7: 7 folds: 128 layers, about 1.3 cm. This is roughly where bare hands give up.
pow.foldCmp10: 10 folds: 1024 layers, about 10 cm — the length of a mobile phone.
pow.foldCmp14: 14 folds: more than 1.6 m — taller than you are.
pow.foldCmp20: 20 folds: about 105 m — longer than a football pitch.
pow.foldCmp23: 23 folds: about 840 m — taller than any building in the world.
pow.foldCmp30: 30 folds: about 107 km — the edge of space is usually drawn at 100 km.
pow.foldCmp42: 42 folds: about 440 000 km — past the Moon, which is 384 000 km away.
pow.defFoldRecord: In reality the paper runs out: nobody can fold a plain sheet more than eight times. The record is {{folds}} folds, set in {{year}}: Britney Gallivan managed it with a {{km}} km long strip of toilet paper.
pow.defTrapNote: (−2)⁴ and −2⁴ are not the same. With the bracket the minus belongs to the base, so it is a product of four negative numbers: positive. Without the bracket the exponent only applies to the 2 and the minus stays outside.
pow.defHint: The bracket says the minus sign is part of the base. Without it the powering comes first, and only then does the minus go in front of the result.
pow.negIntro: What is 2⁰? Multiplying something "zero times" means nothing, so the definition gives no answer. Instead let us walk down the exponents: each step lowers the exponent by one and divides the value by the base. Pick a base and see what happens when you carry that step on below 0.
pow.negDef1: Zeroth power: a⁰ = 1 for every a ≠ 0. This is not an arbitrary decision: dividing a¹ = a by a once more gives exactly 1, so it is the only value that keeps the pattern. 0⁰ is not defined.
pow.negDef2: Negative exponent: a⁻ⁿ = 1 / aⁿ, where a ≠ 0. A negative exponent therefore means a reciprocal, not a negative number: 2⁻³ = 1/8, which is positive.
pow.negZeroNote: Find the row with exponent 0: the value there is 1, whichever base you picked. Below it come the negative exponents, and each step divides once more — which is how they turn into fractions.
pow.negTenNote: This is especially handy for powers of 10: 10⁻¹ = 0.1, 10⁻² = 0.01, 10⁻³ = 0.001. The negative exponent tells you which decimal place the 1 sits in. This is what normal form uses.
pow.negTask: Write 5⁻² as a fraction. Give the numerator and the denominator.
pow.negHint: Work out 5 squared first, then turn the fraction upside down.
pow.lawsIntro: 2³ · 2² = ? Do not multiply anything, just count: three 2s on the left, two on the right, five together. The picture is not an example, it is a proof — it works the same way for every exponent. Pick a law, a base and the exponents, and count the little squares.
pow.lawsPictureAria: The factors arranged in groups, {{total}} little squares in total.
pow.lawsResult_product: The same base stands on the left and on the right, just in different numbers. Put side by side there are as many factors as the sum of the two exponents — which is why the exponents add up.
pow.lawsResult_quotient: The same number stands above and below the fraction bar, so they cancel in pairs. Exactly as many factors are left on top as the difference of the two exponents.
pow.lawsResult_power: Every row is one bracket, and every row holds the same number of factors. So the number of factors is the product of the two exponents.
pow.lawsResult_productBase: Regrouped, all the a's go into one group and all the b's into the other. That is why a power of a product may be taken factor by factor.
pow.lawsResult_quotientBase: Regrouped, all the a's go into the numerator and all the b's into the denominator. That is why a power of a quotient may be taken top and bottom separately.
pow.lawsTrap: There is, however, no rule for a sum. ({{a}} + {{b}})² comes to {{whole}}, while {{a}}² + {{b}}² is only {{parts}}. In the same way aᵐ + aⁿ cannot be merged into one power: the laws are about multiplying and dividing, not about adding.
pow.lawsTask: Write this as a single power: (3²)³ · 3⁴ : 3⁵. What is the exponent?
pow.lawsHint: Power of a power first: 2 · 3 = 6. Then the multiplication adds 4 and the division subtracts 5.
pow.sciIntro: The Earth weighs 5 972 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 kg and a hydrogen atom is 0.0000000001 m across. Numbers like these are awkward to write down and next to impossible to compare: you end up counting zeros one by one. Move the point with the slider until a single digit is left in front of it, and watch the exponent of 10.
pow.sciDef: Normal form: a number written as a · 10ᵏ, where a falls between 1 and 10 (1 ≤ a < 10) and k is a whole number. a does not have to be whole: it is usually a decimal such as 1.496 or 5.2, with exactly one non-zero digit before the point.
pow.sciPreset_earthSun: Distance from the Earth to the Sun
pow.sciPreset_redCell: The diameter of a red blood cell
pow.sciPreset_hydrogen: The diameter of a hydrogen atom
pow.sciDigitsAria: The digits of the number, with the decimal point after digit {{before}}.
pow.sciPickShift: How many places do we move the point?
pow.sciResultOk: There it is: exactly one non-zero digit stands in front of the point. The exponent of 10 counts how many places the point moved — and the value of the number has not changed by a hair.
pow.sciResultNo: Keep moving the point: normal form wants exactly one non-zero digit in front of it. Meanwhile the exponent of 10 counts how many places the point has moved.
pow.sciSignNote: The exponent is positive for large numbers and negative for numbers below 1. On a calculator display this shows up as 1.496E8: the same thing, with the "· 10" left out.
pow.sciHint: Move the point four places to the right, so that it lands in front of the 5. That is why the exponent is negative.
pow.sqrtIntro: A square plot has an area of 49 m². How long is its side? 7 m, because 7 · 7 = 49. Asking the question backwards like this is taking a root: the square is given, the side is wanted. Drag the slider and watch the side grow with the area — and which two whole numbers it falls between when it does not come out exactly.
pow.sqrtDef: Square root: the square root of a number a ≥ 0 is the non-negative number whose square is a. It is written √a. For example √49 = 7, because 7 ≥ 0 and 7² = 49.
pow.sqrtAria: A square of area {{area}} units, with a side of {{side}} units.
pow.sqrtExactNote: {{area}} is a perfect square, so its root is a whole number: √{{area}} = {{root}}. The side of the square can be labelled exactly.
pow.sqrtBetweenNote: √{{area}} is not a whole number: it falls between {{lo}} and {{hi}}, because {{loSq}} < {{area}} < {{hiSq}}. Always run this check before believing what the machine printed.
pow.sqrtSumTrap: A root cannot be split across a sum. √({{a}} + {{b}}) comes to {{whole}}, but √{{a}} + √{{b}} is already {{parts}}. This is the most common mistake in the whole topic — splitting works for a product and a quotient, never for a sum.
pow.sqrtHint: Under the root sign the addition comes first. On the other side you take two separate roots and only then add them up.
pow.nthIntro: A cube has a volume of 27 cm³, so its edge is 3 cm, because 3³ = 27. That is the cube root, and there are fifth roots in just the same way. But what if the exponent were not a whole number but a fraction? Pick a root index and a number: the same value appears as ⁿ√a and as a^(1/n).
pow.nthDef1: n-th root: the n-th root of a number a is the number whose n-th power is a. It is written ⁿ√a. For even n we need a ≥ 0 and take the non-negative root; for odd n any a works, for example ∛(−8) = −2.
pow.nthDef2: Fractional exponent: the exponent 1/n means taking the n-th root, and the exponent m/n means a root and a power together — it does not matter which you do first. The base here is a positive number.
pow.nthResult: Whatever you set, the two writings give the same number: ⁿ√a and a^(1/n) are one and the same. It is not a matter of agreement — it is the only reading under which the "power of a power" law stays true.
pow.nthWhy: Apply the "power of a power" rule to the exponent 1/2. The exponents multiply, so the result is the base itself. In other words, the power with exponent 1/2 is the number whose square is the base — and that is exactly what the square root means. No other choice is left.
pow.nthTask: Work this out: 16 to the power 3/4.
pow.nthHint: The fourth root first: the fourth root of 16 is 2. Then cube it: 2³ = 8.

alg.q3: Why is (a + b)² not a² + b²?
alg.q5: Completing the square: where is the lowest point of the parabola?
alg.trickIntro: Think of a number. Add 5, multiply by 2, subtract 10, divide by 2 — and you get back exactly the number you thought of. The secret is to write a letter where that number would go: x can be any number at all. Pick a trick, set what you thought of, and follow the two columns.
alg.trickDef1: Algebraic expression (an expression with letters): an expression built from numbers, letters and operation signs, for example 2x + 10 or 3a − b. The letter stands in for a number we do not know, or one that could be anything.
alg.trickDef2: Variable: the letter in the expression. x is not a secret particular number; it is a place any number can be written into.
alg.trickStep_addNext: Add the number one bigger than this one
alg.trickStep_subSecret: Subtract the number you thought of
alg.trickEndsX: The last row is x, so the number you thought of always comes back. That is why the trick works for any number at all — without trying a single particular one.
alg.trickEndsConst: There is no x in the last row, only {{value}}. The result therefore does not depend on the number you thought of: everyone gets the same one, whatever they started with.
alg.trickTask: Here is a new trick: think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 8, divide by 4, and finally subtract the number you thought of. What always comes out?
alg.trickHint: Write it with x: 4x, then 4x + 8, then x + 2, and subtract the x at the end.
alg.expandIntro: (x + 3)(x + 2) is the area of a rectangle: one side is x + 3, the other x + 2. Measure it in one piece and you get the product; measure it piece by piece and you get the sum of the parts. The two agree — which is why every term inside a bracket has to be multiplied. Switch mode, drag the sliders, and watch the rectangle fall apart.
alg.expandDef1: Identity: an equality that holds for every value of the letters. 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12 is an identity: whatever you write in place of x, the two sides are equal.
alg.expandDef2: Factoring out: expanding read backwards. If the same factor appears in every term, we take it out in front of the bracket: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3), 4x² + 6x = 2x(2x + 3).
alg.expandPickK: The number in front of the bracket
alg.expandAria_one: A rectangle with one side {{k}} and the other x + {{a}}. It is split in two: one part is the x part, the other is the number.
alg.expandAria_two: A rectangle split into four parts: the big x² square, an x rectangle beside it and another below it with sides {{a}} and {{b}}, and the product of the two numbers in the corner.
alg.expandResultOne: The same rectangle measured two ways: in one piece, or piece by piece. The two always agree, which is why every term inside the bracket has to be multiplied by the factor in front of it — not just the first one.
alg.expandResultTwo: The four pieces collected: the middle term is {{a}} + {{b}} = {{sum}}, and the last one is {{a}} · {{b}} = {{product}}. Drag the sliders: those two rules survive every setting.
alg.expandLikeNote: Only like terms can be collected — the ones whose letter part is the same. In the picture the two x pieces add up, while the x² and the number stay apart: 3x² + 5x is neither 8x⁵ nor 8x³.
alg.expandTask: Expand: (x + 4)(x + 5) = x² + □x + □. What goes in the two boxes?
alg.expandHint: The middle coefficient is the sum of 4 and 5, and the last number is their product.
alg.squareIntro: What is 31²? You can do it in your head: 31 = 30 + 1, and the square (30 + 1)² falls into four pieces — 30², twice 30 · 1, and 1², that is 900 + 60 + 1 = 961. The picture shows exactly those four pieces. Drag the sliders and press the part buttons to find where the 2ab in the middle comes from.
alg.squareDef: Named identity: an identity used so often that it is worth knowing by heart. The three most important ones are (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² and (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
alg.squareAriaPlus: A square of side {{a}} + {{b}} split into four parts: an a² square, two identical a · b rectangles and a b² square.
alg.squareAriaMinus: A square of side {{a}} with the (a − b)² square in its top left corner, a strip of width {{b}} beside it and another below it, and the b² square in the bottom right corner.
alg.squareReadPlus: The big square has side {{a}} + {{b}}, and its area is the sum of the four parts. The two identical rectangles are what make the 2ab: that is why (a + b)² = a² + b² is not true.
alg.squareReadMinus: The big square is the a², and the little square of side {{rest}} in the top left corner is the (a − b)² we are after. The two strips of width {{b}} come to 2ab together, but where they overlap the b² was taken away twice, so it has to be given back once.
alg.squareMentalTitle: In your head: squaring two-digit numbers
alg.squareMentalNote: We always work from the nearest round ten, so the small part is at most 5 and its square at most 25 — little enough to keep in your head.
alg.squareTask: Work it out in your head: 52² = ?
alg.diffIntro: What is 99 · 101? Write it like this: (100 − 1)(100 + 1). In the picture we cut a corner of side b out of a square of side a, and rearrange the L shape that is left into a single rectangle with sides a + b and a − b. The same area in two shapes. Press the Rearrange button.
alg.diffRule: The third named identity: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². When the brackets are expanded, the two mixed terms, −ab and +ab, cancel each other, which is why only the difference of the two squares is left.
alg.diffAriaBefore: A square of side {{a}} with a square of side {{b}} missing from its bottom right corner. The remaining L shape is split into two rectangles.
alg.diffAriaAfter: The same two rectangles laid end to end: one rectangle {{a}} + {{b}} wide and {{a}} − {{b}} high.
alg.diffRead: The rearranged rectangle is {{width}} units wide and {{height}} units high, so its area is {{value}} — exactly the difference of the two squares.
alg.diffPickD: How far we step from it
alg.diffTask: Work it out in your head: 39 · 41 = ?
alg.diffHint: 39 = 40 − 1 and 41 = 40 + 1, so 40² − 1² is what is left.
alg.completeIntro: x² + 6x + 5 is not a perfect square, but it is nearly one: x² + 6x + 9 would be, because it is (x + 3)². So let us add the 9 and take it straight back off again. (x + 3)² is never negative and its smallest value is 0 — which is why the new shape hands you the lowest point of the parabola. Move the sliders and watch it travel.
alg.completeDef: Completing the square: putting an expression of the form x² + px + q into the form (x + h)² + k. Here h is half of p, and k is the correction the added h² calls for: k = q − h².
alg.completeAria: A square of side x with a strip of width {{h}} beside it and another below it, and in the corner, drawn with a dashed line, the missing little square of area {{square}}.
alg.completeNoPicture: The picture shows the case of a positive p.
alg.completeVertex: The lowest point: at x = {{x}} the value is {{k}}. Both numbers were read straight off the completed square, with no working out at all.
alg.completeTask: Complete the square: x² − 8x + 3 = (x + □)² + □. Write in the two numbers, with their signs.
alg.completeHint: Half of −8 is −4, and the (−4)² = 16 has to be taken away again.

prop.q3: Growing together, but proportional? The graph gives it away

prop.inverseIntro: You are sharing a pizza of 24 slices. Two of you get 12 slices each, six of you get 4, twelve of you get 2: twice as many people get half as much each. Here it is not the quotient but the product that stays constant. Drag the slider and watch the third statistic — it does not budge.
prop.inverseDef: Inverse proportion: two quantities are inversely proportional if whenever one grows by some factor, the other shrinks to the same fraction of itself. Their product is then constant: x · y = k, that is, y = k / x.
prop.inverseLblX_pizza: How many of you there are
prop.inverseConstant: Their product is the same wherever you put the slider: {{x}} · {{y}} = {{k}}. That constant is the mark of an inverse proportion.
prop.inverseDoubled: {{x}} → {{x2}}: twice as many, {{y}} → {{y2}}: half as much.
prop.inverseNote: The graph is a curve that flattens out but never reaches the axes: however many of you there are, everyone gets something, and however little each gets, there is some number of you.
prop.inverseTask: Six workers paint a school in 10 days. How many days does the same job take four workers?
prop.inverseHint: First work out the whole job in worker-days: 6 · 10. Then divide that by 4.
prop.graphsIntro: Many quantities change together without being proportional: a taxi fare grows with the distance, but there is a fixed charge; a person's height grows with their age, but no formula ties them. Proportion is stricter than that. Pick a situation and see which curve lights up next to it — and which one lights up none at all.
prop.graphsDef1: Quadratic proportion: one quantity is proportional to the square of the other: y = k · x². If x doubles, y grows fourfold.
prop.graphsDef2: Square-root proportion: one quantity is proportional to the square root of the other: y = k · √x. If x grows fourfold, y only doubles.
prop.graphKind_linear: a line, but not a proportion: y = k · x + b
prop.graphAria_direct: A straight line rising steadily from the origin.
prop.graphAria_inverse: A falling curve that flattens out but never reaches the axes.
prop.graphAria_linear: A straight line rising steadily, starting above the origin rather than at it.
prop.graphAria_square: A curve rising ever more steeply: the right half of a parabola.
prop.graphAria_root: A rising curve that flattens out but never turns back.
prop.graphsPickPrompt: Pick a situation and the curve that belongs to it lights up.
prop.sit_apples: the price of apples against their weight
prop.sit_taxi: a taxi fare against the distance
prop.sit_squareArea: the area of a square against its side
prop.sit_areaSide: the side of a square against its area
prop.sit_workersDays: the time of a job against the number of workers
prop.sit_phoneMonths: a phone bill against the number of months (fixed monthly fee)
prop.sitWhy_apples: Twice as many apples cost twice as much, and 0 kg costs 0 Ft: direct proportion.
prop.sitWhy_taxi: There is a fixed charge, so 0 km is not 0 Ft: a line, but not through the origin — so not a proportion. A bill with a fixed monthly fee does exactly the same: the fixed part always spoils the proportion.
prop.sitWhy_speedTime: Twice the speed means half the time: their product, the distance, stays constant.
prop.sitWhy_squareArea: Twice the side gives four times the area: quadratic.
prop.sitWhy_areaSide: Four times the area gives twice the side: a square-root connection.
prop.sitWhy_ageHeight: They grow together, but no formula ties them: none of the curves.
prop.graphsTask: What connects the two quantities? Decide it for all eight.
prop.graphsHint: Ask yourself: if one quantity doubles, what happens to the other? It doubles, it halves, it grows fourfold — or none of these.
prop.percentIntro: A coat of 15 000 Ft is on sale at 20% off. Percent means hundredth: 20% is 20/100, that is 0.2. Three numbers always travel together — the whole, the size of the percentage and the amount taken off — and any two of them give the third. Pick the one that is missing and watch the formula and the bar.
prop.percentDef1: Base: the whole the percentage is taken of. In the coat example it is 15 000 Ft.
prop.percentDef2: Rate: the size of the percentage, the number in front of the percent sign. In the example it is 20.
prop.percentDef3: Percentage value: the given percentage of the base, the amount we end up with. In the example it is 3000 Ft.
prop.unknown_value: I am looking for the value
prop.unknown_rate: I am looking for the rate
prop.unknown_base: I am looking for the base
prop.percentSentence: {{rate}}% of {{base}} Ft is {{value}} Ft. The same three numbers, whichever of them you set out to find.
prop.percentBarAria: A horizontal bar: its whole length is the base, its shaded part is the percentage value.
prop.percentTask: A pair of shoes of 24 000 Ft is sold for 18 000 Ft. What percentage is the discount?
prop.percentHint: The discount in forints is 6000. The base is the original price, 24 000.
prop.changeIntro: The price of something goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Do we get the original price back? No: the drop is computed from the raised price. Set the two steps and watch the Multiplier column — two changes one after the other are two multiplications, and multiplications do not add up.
prop.changeDef: Percentage point: the difference of two percentages. From 3% to 4% the change is one percentage point, even though that is a third more interest.
prop.changeRule: The multiplier: a rise of p% is multiplying by (1 + p/100), a drop of p% is multiplying by (1 − p/100). This is how several changes melt into a single product — and exactly why the percentages cannot simply be added.
prop.changePoints: The change in percentage points: {{diff}}. The change in percent: {{pct}}% — the new rate is {{ratio}}% of the old one. These two are what the news mixes up most often.
prop.changeTask: The price of something rose by 25% and then fell by 20%. What percentage of the original price is it now?
prop.changeAnswerLabel: As a percentage of the original price
prop.interestIntro: If you put 100 000 Ft in the bank at 5% a year, after one year you have 105 000 Ft. In the second year you get 5% of that, so not 5000 but 5250 Ft. The money grows by the same multiplier year after year. Set the rate and the years, and watch how far the two curves come apart.
prop.interestDef: Interest: the amount a bank pays for the money kept there (or the amount asked for a loan). Interest rate: the interest as a percentage, counted for one year.
prop.interestGap: Over {{years}} years compound interest gives {{diff}} Ft more than simple interest — and the gap widens faster with every further year.
prop.interestTask: You put 200 000 Ft in the bank at 4% a year. How much money will you have after two years?
prop.interestHint: Multiply by 1.04 twice, not by 1.08 once.

lin.stepMoveX: Move the x terms to the left.
lin.stepMoveNum: Move the numbers to the right.
lin.stepDivide: Divide both sides by the coefficient of x.
lin.stepDivideFlip: We are dividing by a negative number, so the sign turns around.
lin.stepExpress: Express y from one of the equations.
lin.stepSubstitute: Write it into the other equation.
lin.stepBack: Substitute back, and the other unknown comes out.
lin.stepMultiply: Multiply the equation so the coefficients of y become opposites.
lin.stepAddRows: Add the two equations: y drops out.
lin.balanceIntro: Picture a balance scale in equilibrium: on the left three identical boxes of unknown weight and two one-kilo weights, on the right one box and eight kilos. Take the same thing off both sides and it stays level — that is exactly how an equation is solved. Your goal is to leave a single box on one side: then the other side tells you what it weighs.
lin.balanceDef: The balance principle: if we do the same thing to both sides of an equation — add or subtract the same amount, multiply or divide by the same number other than zero — the solution of the equation does not change.
lin.balanceAria: A balance scale in equilibrium. The equation right now: {{equation}}.
lin.balanceWhyDisabled: A greyed-out move cannot be made right now: only moves that work on both sides at once are allowed.
lin.balanceStepRemoveX: Took one box off both sides.
lin.balanceSolved: One box weighs {{x}} kg. Check: 3 · {{x}} + 2 = {{x}} + 8 — both sides come to {{left}}.
lin.balanceHint: Subtract 2x from both sides, add 7 to both sides, then divide both sides by 3.
lin.graphIntro: The two sides of an equation are two separate expressions, and both can be drawn: y = x + 1 is one line, y = −x + 7 the other. Where the two lines cross, the two sides are equal — the x-coordinate of the crossing point is the solution. Move the two lines with the sliders and watch what happens to the crossing point when they turn parallel, or land on top of each other.
lin.graphResult_one: The two lines cross at one point: x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}. There is exactly one solution.
lin.graphResult_none: The two lines are parallel: they have no common point, so the equation has no solution.
lin.graphResult_all: The two lines coincide: every point is common to both, so every number is a solution — the two sides are the same expression.
lin.graphNote: A picture can only be read approximately: if the crossing point is somewhere around 2.33, that will not tell you it is exactly 7/3. The exact solution comes from the balance principle; the picture is for estimating and for checking.
lin.graphTask: Read it off the picture: where do the two lines cross? Give the solution.
lin.graphHint: Look for the x where both lines are at the same height.
lin.ineqIntro: 3 < 5, that is true. Multiply both sides by −1: −3 and −5 — now −3 is the bigger one, so the sign has turned around. For an inequality the balance principle works almost exactly as it does for an equation; this one move is the thing to remember. Pick an inequality and drag the test point onto the half-line: putting it back into the original shows at once whether it belongs there.
lin.ineqLineAria: Number line: the solution is the half-line x {{rel}} {{bound}}, with the test point on it.
lin.ineqForget: What if we forgot to turn the sign?
lin.ineqForgetNote: The half-line in the second colour is the wrong answer. Drag the test point onto it: it says something different from the original inequality.
lin.ineqNoFlipHere: In this example we divide by a positive number, so the sign stays — there is nothing to get wrong here.
lin.ineqTrue: true, so {{x}} is in the solution set.
lin.ineqFalse: false, so {{x}} is not in the solution set.
lin.ineqRule: The sign turns around if you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number. Multiplying by a positive number, or adding and subtracting anything, leaves it as it is.
lin.ineqHint: Try x = 0 in the original: 5 ≥ −4 is true, so 0 must be in the solution set.
lin.systemsIntro: Two numbers add up to 10 and differ by 4 — which two numbers are they? Two unknowns need two equations: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. Both methods come to the same thing: make one unknown disappear so that a one-unknown equation is left. Pick a method and step through it; below the steps, the same system is two lines.
lin.systemsDef: System of equations: several equations sharing the same unknowns, all of which have to hold at once; its solution is the pair (x; y) that makes every one of them true.
lin.systemsShopText: Three pens and two notebooks cost 1900 Ft, one pen and one notebook cost 800 Ft. x is the price of a pen, y the price of a notebook.
lin.systemsResult: The solution is x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}: this pair makes both equations true, and it is exactly where the two lines cross in the picture. The other method leads to the same place.
lin.systemsTask: Two numbers add up to 12 and differ by 2. Which two numbers are they?
lin.systemsHint: Add the two equations: y drops out and 2x = 14 is left.
lin.modelIntro: Two towns are 180 km apart. A car sets off from one of them at 60 km/h, and at the same moment another sets off from the other at 30 km/h, towards it — when do they meet? There is not a single equation in the text; we have to write it: let t be the time elapsed in hours, and then 60t + 30t = 180. Drag the time and watch where the picture and the equation meet.
lin.modelDef: Mathematical model: the word problem translated into the language of mathematics — the data, the unknown, and the relation between them written as an equation.
lin.modelAria: A road from 0 to 180 km: after {{t}} hours the first car is at {{car1}} km and the second at {{car2}} km.
lin.modelLine: t = {{t}} hours: 60 · {{t}} + 30 · {{t}} = {{sum}} km, still {{gap}} km short of the 180.
lin.modelMet: t = 2 hours: 120 + 60 = 180 km — they have met. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.modelPassed: t = {{t}} hours: they have already passed each other, together they have covered {{sum}} km. More than the 180 km is not a sensible answer to the question.
lin.modelSteps: The five steps: 1. gather the data, 2. choose the unknown, 3. write the equation, 4. solve it, 5. check it against the original text and answer.
lin.modelTask: The same problem, but the second car goes at 40 km/h. After how many hours do they meet?
lin.modelHint: Write the equation the same way: 60t + 40t = 180.
lin.problemsIntro: The same five steps work in other situations too; only the relation is different. For joint work we add up how much of the job each of them does in an hour; for mixing we add up the amount of the dissolved substance, not the percentages. Use the slider to find the value where the two sides agree, then look at how the equation gives the same thing.
lin.workText: Anna paints a room in 6 hours, Bence in 3. How long does it take the two of them together?
lin.workDone: t = 2 hours: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1, the room is done. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.problemsWorkRule: Joint work: if alone they finish in t₁ and t₂ hours, together they finish in t hours, where t/t₁ + t/t₂ = 1.
lin.mixText: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution, and we have a 20% and a 50% one. How much should we take of the 20% one?
lin.mixLine: x = {{x}} l: 0.2 · {{x}} + 0.5 · {{rest}} = {{amount}} l of substance, which is {{pct}}%.
lin.mixDone: x = 2 l: 0.4 + 2 = 2.4 litres of substance in 6 litres, which is exactly 40%. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.problemsMixRule: Mixing: the dissolved substance does not go anywhere: the amounts in the parts add up to the amount in the mixture.
lin.data_v1: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution. We have a 20% one and a stronger one. How much should we take of the 20% one?
lin.data_v2: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution, and we have a 20% and a 50% one. The solutions cost 300 Ft a litre. How much should we take of the 20% one?
lin.data_v3: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution, so we pour together 3 litres of the 20% one and 4 litres of the 50% one. What will the strength of the mixture be?
lin.dataOpt_redundant: there is a spare datum, but it can be solved
lin.problemsTask: What is wrong with each of these texts?
lin.problemsHint: Try to write the equation for each: the first one is short of a number, the second leaves one datum unused, and in the third 3 + 4 = 7 litres, where 6 were wanted.

quad.q1: Why must you not divide by x? The lost root
quad.q2: Two numbers with a given sum and product: factoring
quad.q3: Where does the quadratic formula come from?
quad.q4: What does the discriminant tell you? The parabola and the x-axis
quad.q5: When is x² − x − 6 negative? An inequality in the picture
quad.q6: From x⁴ to a quadratic: the new unknown
quad.q7: Which root is the answer? A garden and a ball
quad.stepURoots: The roots we get for u.
quad.stepReject: A square is never negative: this u is rejected.
quad.stepXRoots: The real roots of the original equation.
quad.lostrootIntro: A number's square is exactly four times the number: x² = 4x. It is tempting to divide both sides by x, and out comes x = 4 — except that 0 was an answer too, and it has just vanished. The right route is factoring: x(x − 4) = 0. Try both candidates in the original equation.
quad.lostrootDef1: Quadratic equation: an equation that can be brought to the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b and c are given numbers and a ≠ 0.
quad.lostrootDef2: Equivalence-preserving step: a step after which the equation has exactly the same solutions — dividing by an expression that contains the unknown is not one, because a root can be lost that way.
quad.lostrootCheck: x = {{x}}: the left side is {{left}}, the right side is {{right}} — the two sides agree, so this is a root. {{fate}}
quad.lostrootFate_lost: And dividing by x lost it.
quad.lostrootHint: Do not divide by x: move everything to one side and take x out — x(x − 3) = 0.
quad.factorIntro: The left side of x² − 5x + 6 = 0 can be factored: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, and a product is zero only if one of its factors is — so x = 2 or x = 3. It works backwards too: set the two roots and watch the coefficients follow.
quad.factorDef: Root-factor form: the quadratic written with its roots, ax² + bx + c = a(x − x₁)(x − x₂), where x₁ and x₂ are the roots of the equation. If the equation has no root, it has no such form either.
quad.factorResult: Sum: {{sum}} = {{sumValue}}, so b = {{b}}. Product: {{prod}} = {{prodValue}}, so c = {{c}}. And the curve crosses the horizontal axis at exactly those two roots.
quad.factorRule: A product is zero if and only if at least one of its factors is zero. That is why the solving is over the moment the left side turns into a product.
quad.factorHint: Look for two numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is 7.
quad.formulaIntro: You do not have to complete the square from scratch for every equation: do it once on the general ax² + bx + c = 0 and you get a formula that only needs the three numbers written into it. The derivation runs in two columns — the letters on the left, the same move on one concrete equation on the right. Pick an equation and see what the formula gives.
quad.formulaDef1: The quadratic formula: the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are x₁,₂ = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a). The ± sign means we work it out once with a plus and once with a minus: that is what gives the two roots.
quad.formulaDef2: Discriminant: the expression under the root sign, D = b² − 4ac. If D > 0 there are two different roots; if D = 0 there is one (double) root; if D < 0 there is no real root.
quad.parDivideOne: Divide by a — here a = 1, so nothing changes.
quad.parFormula: Subtract the b/2a term: this is the quadratic formula.
quad.parNoRoot: A square is never negative: there is no real root.
quad.formulaHint: D = 25 − 16 = 9, whose root is 3, and the denominator is 2 · 2.
quad.discIntro: Draw the function y = ax² + bx + c and you get a parabola; the roots of the equation are where it crosses the x-axis, because that is where y = 0. Move the three coefficients and watch the discriminant and the picture at the same time: the parabola either crosses the axis twice, touches it once, or never reaches it.
quad.discNoRoot: The parabola never reaches the x-axis, so the equation has no real root.
quad.discRule: D and the parabola: D > 0 — two crossing points; D = 0 — the parabola touches the x-axis; D < 0 — the parabola never reaches the x-axis. The roots can only be read off the picture approximately; the exact value comes from the formula.
quad.discTask: For which c does x² + 4x + c = 0 have exactly one root?
quad.discHint: One root means D = 0, that is, 16 − 4c = 0.
quad.ineqIntro: When is x² − x − 6 negative? The roots of the parabola are −2 and 3, and between them the curve runs below the x-axis, outside them above it — so the answer is −2 < x < 3. Pick an inequality and drag the test point: the shaded stretch is where the inequality holds.
quad.ineqLineAria: Number line: the solution set is {{set}}, with the test point on it.
quad.ineqSet_between: Between the two roots the parabola is below the axis.
quad.ineqSet_outside: Outside the two roots the parabola is above the axis.
quad.ineqSet_allBut: The parabola touches the axis: everywhere except that one place it is on the right side.
quad.ineqSet_none: The parabola never reaches the axis, so there is no solution.
quad.ineqSet_all: The parabola is on the right side everywhere: every number is a solution.
quad.ineqSet_only: A single number is the solution: where the parabola touches the axis.
quad.ineqTrue: true, it is in the solution set.
quad.ineqFalse: false, it is not in the solution set.
quad.ineqRule: A parabola opening upwards (a > 0) is negative between its two roots and positive outside them. If it has no root, it is positive everywhere.
quad.ineqHint: The roots are −2 and 2. Try x = 0 and x = 3.
quad.reduceIntro: x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 is a fourth-degree equation, and you can still solve it, because only x² and x⁴ appear in it. Call x² by the name u: what is left is u² − 5u + 4 = 0, an ordinary quadratic. At the end you have to come back to x, and that is where marks are lost: a u that came out negative has no x behind it. Step through the three examples.
quad.reduceDef: Introducing a new unknown (substitution): we give a repeated part of the equation a single letter, solve the simpler equation that results, and then work the original unknown back out of the values we got — rejecting on the way any value the substituted expression cannot take.
quad.reduceRejectNote: One of the u values was rejected: x² is never negative.
quad.reduceTask: How many real roots does x⁴ − 10x² + 9 = 0 have?
quad.reduceHint: The roots for u are 1 and 9, and every positive u gives two values of x.
quad.wordIntro: One side of a rectangular garden is 3 metres longer than the other, and its area is 40 m². Let x be the shorter side: x(x + 3) = 40, which tidies to x² + 3x − 40 = 0, with roots 5 and −8. Mathematically −8 is a root, but a side cannot be negative. Drag the slider in both problems and see which root makes sense.
quad.wordGardenAria: A rectangular garden: its shorter side is {{x}} metres, the longer one {{long}} metres, its area {{area}} square metres.
quad.gardenLine: x = {{x}} m, so the area is {{x}} · {{long}} = {{area}} m².
quad.gardenDone: x = 5 m: 5 · 8 = 40 m². That is the answer: 5 m and 8 m.
quad.gardenReject: −8 is a root as well, but a side cannot be negative, so we reject it.

quad.ballDone: t = 4 s: h = 0, the ball has landed.
quad.ballBelow: t is more than 4: the formula gives a negative height, but the ball is already on the ground — the model no longer holds here.
quad.ballStart: t = 0 is the moment it was thrown, so the answer is t = 4.
quad.wordTask: Two consecutive positive whole numbers multiply to 56. Which two numbers are they?
quad.wordHint: The equation is x(x + 1) = 56, and one of its roots is negative.

fn.assignIntro: To every pupil we assign their shoe size. To every country its capital. To every person their siblings. All three are assignments, but only the first two are functions: some people have no sibling at all and some have two. Pick an example and move the arrows around — the card says when the one-arrow rule breaks.
fn.assignDef1: Single-valued assignment: every element of the first set has exactly one element assigned to it — exactly one arrow leaves every point. An assignment like that is what we call a function.
fn.assignDef2: One-to-one assignment: single-valued, and on top of that no element on the right receives more than one arrow — which is exactly when the arrows can be turned around.

fn.readIntro: The temperature of a winter day, hour by hour: coldest at 4 in the morning, warmest at 2 in the afternoon, and crossing 0 degrees twice on the way. A graph says all of that at a glance — if you know what to look for. Use the buttons to light up one property at a time, and the slider to read the temperature at any hour.
fn.readDef1: Zero: an x where the value of the function is 0 — this is where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.
fn.readDef2: Extreme value: the largest value of the function is its maximum, the smallest its minimum; the x where it takes that value is the place of the maximum or minimum.
fn.readDef3: Increasing and decreasing: on a stretch the function is increasing if the graph climbs from left to right, and decreasing if it falls.
fn.read_zeros: Zeros: {{list}}. This is where the curve crosses the horizontal axis.
fn.read_up: Increasing: {{spans}}. The graph climbs from left to right here.
fn.read_down: Decreasing: {{spans}}. The graph falls from left to right here.
fn.readTask: On which interval is the function increasing?
fn.readHint: Follow the curve from left to right and see which stretch climbs.
fn.linearIntro: A taxi fare, a phone bill, a temperature in Fahrenheit — all the same formula: f(x) = mx + b. Its graph is always a straight line, and both numbers can be read off it. Move the sliders and watch the step in the picture: one unit to the right, m units up.
fn.linearDef1: Linear function: a function of the form f(x) = mx + b, where m and b are given numbers; its graph is a straight line.
fn.linearDef2: Slope and intercept: m is the slope — how much the value changes when x grows by one; b is the intercept — the value of the function at x = 0.
fn.linearResult: b = {{b}}: this is where the line meets the y-axis. m = {{m}}: one step to the right and it {{dir}} by {{step}} units.
fn.linearResultFlat: b = {{b}}: this is where the line meets the y-axis. m = 0: the line is horizontal, every x has the same value.
fn.linearWhyB: This is b: the value of the function at x = 0.
fn.linearWhyM: One step to the right: the value changed by m.
fn.linearTask: The line passes through (0; −1) and (2; 3). What are m and b?
fn.linearHint: b is the value of the function at x = 0. m is the change in y divided by the change in x between the two points.
fn.elemIntro: Three functions are worth knowing thoroughly, because they keep coming back: x², √x and 1/x. Turn the usual question around: instead of asking what f(x) is, ask how many x-es belong to a given value. Move the horizontal line with the slider — however many times it meets the curve, that is how many solutions f(x) = c has.
fn.elemDef1: The square function: f(x) = x², defined for every real number, its values are non-negative, and its graph is a parabola.
fn.elemDef2: The square root function: f(x) = √x, defined only for x ≥ 0, increasing all the way, with non-negative values.
fn.elemDef3: The inverse proportion function: f(x) = 1/x, defined for every x except 0, never equal to 0, and its graph is a hyperbola of two branches.
fn.elemSolutions_0: No x at all belongs to the value {{c}} — the line never reaches the curve.
fn.elemSolutions_1: Exactly one x belongs to the value {{c}}: x = {{x1}}. The line meets the curve in one place.
fn.elemSolutions_2: Two x-es belong to the value {{c}}: x = {{x1}} and x = {{x2}}. The line meets the curve in two places.
fn.elemTask: Which of the functions has no zero?
fn.elemHint: A zero is where the graph touches the x-axis. Which graph never gets there?
fn.transformIntro: If you know the graph of x², you know the graph of (x − 3)² + 2 as well: the same parabola, moved along. One thing does go against the first guess, though: f(x + 3) moves to the left, not to the right — at x = −3 it takes the value f has at 0. Try it with the sliders; the dashed curve is the original.
fn.transformRule: f(x) + c: moves the graph up by c (down for a negative c). f(x + c): moves it left by c (right for a negative c). c · f(x): stretches it c times in the y direction; a negative c mirrors it in the x-axis. |f(x)|: whatever was below the axis comes up above it.
fn.transformPickDy: Shift at the end of the formula (c)
fn.transformSignAria: The sign of the multiplier and the absolute value
fn.transformTask: Which formula gives the graph of x² moved 3 to the right?
fn.transformHint: The lowest point of the new graph is at x = 3. Which formula gives 0 there?
fn.inverseIntro: Celsius turns into Fahrenheit like this: f(x) = 1.8x + 32. And back again? We undo the steps: subtract 32, divide by 1.8. In the picture that is a reflection: every point (x; y) becomes (y; x), so the graph of the reversed function is the mirror image of the original in the line y = x. Drag the slider and watch the point and its mirror image.
fn.inverseDef: Reversed (inverse) assignment: the reverse of a one-to-one assignment f is the assignment that gives back x for every value f(x).
fn.inverseLine: f({{x}}) = {{y}}, and back the other way: f⁻¹({{y}}) = {{x}}. The two curves are mirror images of each other in the dashed line y = x.
fn.inverseSquareNote: x² cannot be turned around as a whole: both 2 and −2 belong to 4, so it is not one-to-one. Look at x ≥ 0 only and every value occurs once, and the reverse of it is exactly √x — which is why the square root function lives on the non-negative numbers.
fn.inverseTask: f(x) = 2x + 6. What does the reversed assignment give for 10?
fn.modelIntro: You set off in the morning: you walk to the stop, wait for the bus, ride it, stand at the traffic lights, then walk to school. A distance–time graph tells the whole story: where the line is horizontal you are standing still, and the steeper it is the faster you are going. fn.modelRule: On a distance–time graph the slope is the speed: a horizontal stretch means standing still, a steeper stretch means going faster.
fn.tripLine: t = {{t}} minutes: you are {{d}} m from home, at {{v}} m per minute — {{what}}.

deriv.title: The derivative: a secant becoming a tangent
deriv.intro1: The derivative answers one question: how steep is the curve at a single point x₀? Think of the curve as a hill you are walking on — the derivative is the slope of the ground exactly under your feet.
deriv.intro2: There's a problem, though. Slope means "rise over run", and that needs two points. One point has no rise and no run. So we cheat in three steps:
deriv.steps12: 1. Pick a second point a small distance h away, at x₀+h. 2. Draw the straight line through both points — the orange secant — and measure its slope, which is just rise over run:
deriv.step3: 3. Shrink h. As the second point slides toward the first, the secant tips over into the dashed tangent — the line that just grazes the curve. The derivative is defined as the value this slope settles on:
deriv.dragNote: Drag the h slider toward 0 and watch it happen. The numbers under the chart update live with your slider.
deriv.texLimitHeading: the limit it is heading for:
deriv.noTangent: No tangent here! Coming from the right the slopes settle on {{right}}, but coming from the left they settle on {{left}}. The two sides disagree, so there is no single answer and f′({{x0}}) does not exist. The curve has a corner at this point.
deriv.tableTitle: The limit, computed like a math student
deriv.tableIntro: "Limit as h approaches 0" sounds abstract, but you can't actually set h = 0 — that would divide by zero. A limit is a promise instead: the closer h gets to 0, the closer the slope gets to one particular number. On paper that promise is just a table. Halve h again and again and watch the right-hand column stop changing. The number it settles on is the derivative.
deriv.tryIt: Try it: pick |x| and slide x₀ to 0. The table refuses to settle, because approaching from the right gives +1 and from the left gives −1 (tick the checkbox to compare the two directions). A corner has no single steepness — that is exactly what "the limit does not exist" means. Then try sin(x) at x₀ = 0 and watch the quotients march to exactly 1: the sine curve leaves the origin at 45°.
deriv.chartAria: Function with secant and tangent lines

integ.title: The integral: rectangles becoming area
integ.intro1: The integral answers: how much area sits between the curve and the x-axis, from a to b? For a rectangle that's easy — width times height. But a curved roof has no ready-made area formula. So, just like with the derivative, we cheat with straight edges, in three steps:
integ.step1: 1. Cut the stretch from a to b into n equal strips. Each strip has width
integ.step2: 2. On each strip, stand a rectangle. Its height is the curve's value at one chosen spot in the strip (the left edge, the middle, or the right edge — your choice above). Rectangles we can measure: each one contributes height × width, and adding all n of them gives the Riemann sum:
integ.step3: 3. Use more, thinner strips. The error lives in the little slivers between the flat rectangle tops and the curve, and thinner strips leave smaller slivers. The integral is the value the total settles on — and the ∫ symbol is literally a stretched-out S, for "sum":
integ.dragNote: Drag n up and watch the orange rectangles melt into the blue area. The numbers under the chart track your sliders.
integ.texLimitHeading: the limit it is heading for:
integ.degenerate: a and b coincide — the area of a zero-width region is 0. Drag them apart.
integ.tableTitle: The limit again, as a table
integ.tableIntro: Same move as on the Derivative tab: a limit is a promise that the numbers settle, and a table makes the promise visible. Each row doubles the number of rectangles. Read down the third column and watch it stop changing — the value it locks onto is the integral.
integ.tryIt: Try it: switch "left edge" to "midpoint" and watch the table settle dramatically faster. Sampling in the middle of each strip lets the rectangle's overshoot on one side cancel its undershoot on the other. Integrate sin(x) from −2 to 2 and get 0: area below the axis counts as negative, and the two halves cancel exactly. And try |x| — the corner that broke the derivative gives the integral no trouble at all, because adding areas doesn't care about a kink the way slopes do. That one-sidedness is why the fundamental theorem of calculus — the statement that derivative and integral undo each other — is a real theorem someone had to prove, not an obvious fact.

fft.subtitle: The Fourier transform's claim: any repeating signal is secretly a sum of simple waves. This page lets you test the claim. Type a function, and the app measures it at N points, finds which waves hide inside (the FFT), throws away all but the strongest ones, and rebuilds the signal from what's left (the inverse FFT). If the rebuilt curve still matches, a few waves were enough to carry the whole signal.
fft.keepLabel: Strongest components to keep (zero-amplitude bins are skipped): {{n}}
fft.timeNote: The blue curve is your function, measured at N points. The dashed orange curve is the rebuilt version — the inverse FFT of only the kept components. Where the two hug each other, those few waves already tell the whole story; drag the "components" slider down and watch the orange curve lose detail first, then shape.
fft.waveNote: Here are the hidden waves the FFT found, drawn one per row so you can see each ingredient on its own — strongest first, all on the same y-scale so heights are comparable. Each label gives the wave's recipe: strength × cos(speed × x + head start). Add every row together, point by point, and you get exactly the dashed orange curve above.
fft.freqNote: The same information as a bar chart — the signal's "recipe card". One bar per possible frequency (bin k = 0 … N/2): its position says how fast that wave repeats, its height says how strongly it is present. Most bars are near zero because most frequencies simply aren't in the signal. Hover a bar for its exact frequency, amplitude and phase; click one to see its value computed step by step below.
fft.binNote: Pick a bin with the +/− buttons, or click any bar in the spectrum above, and watch its value worked out by hand.
fft.resultNote: The recipe in one line — this sum of simple waves is what the inverse FFT actually draws as the dashed curve. The RMS error above says how far that drawing is from your function, averaged over all sample points (0 means a perfect match).

bin.intro: A "bin" is one slot of the transform's output. Bin k asks a single question: how much of the signal is a wave that repeats exactly {{k}} times across the window? To answer it, the DFT compares the signal against that wave, sample by sample: multiply them together and add everything up. Where the signal moves in step with the reference wave the products pile up; where it doesn't, they cancel. The whole definition is one line (the e-power is just shorthand for a cosine and sine pair):

bin.assemble: Now assemble the answer from the two column totals. The cosine total becomes the real part, the sine total (with its sign flipped, from the −i in the definition) becomes the imaginary part:
bin.strength: Those two numbers hold the wave's strength and its shift. The strength (amplitude) is the length of the pair, read off with Pythagoras{{doubled}}:

alias.title: Aliasing: when sampling lies
alias.intro: Everything above rests on one quiet assumption: that N samples are enough to know which wave produced them. This demo is where the assumption breaks. A computer cannot store a smooth curve, only samples of it — here a sine with a frequency you control, sampled at the same 64 evenly spaced points (green dots) no matter how fast it oscillates. To capture a wiggle you need at least 2 samples per cycle: one near a crest, one near a trough. With 64 samples that caps honest measurement at 32 cycles per window. Push beyond it and the samples do not go blank — they lie.
alias.sliderLabel: True frequency: {{k}} cycles per window (Nyquist limit is 32)
alias.verdictNyquist: {{k}} cycles is exactly N/2. A sine at this frequency crosses zero at every single sample point — all 64 measurements read 0, and the wave vanishes without a trace.
alias.verdictFaithful: {{k}} cycles stays at or below N/2 = 32, so every cycle gets at least 2 samples. The measurements describe the wave truthfully, and the energy lands in bin {{bin}}. The two curves are one and the same.
alias.turnsClause_one: {{count}} whole turn between consecutive samples is invisible, and
alias.turnsClause_other: {{count}} whole turns between consecutive samples are invisible, and
alias.verdictFlippedA: what's left over looks like {{bin}} cycles running backwards. The measurements are identical to
alias.verdictFlippedB: , so the energy lands in bin {{bin}}.
alias.verdictWrapped_one: the {{count}} whole turn between consecutive samples is invisible, so the measurements are identical to a {{bin}}-cycle wave. The energy lands in bin {{bin}}.
alias.verdictWrapped_other: the {{count}} whole turns between consecutive samples are invisible, so the measurements are identical to a {{bin}}-cycle wave. The energy lands in bin {{bin}}.
alias.wholeTitle: The whole window — every green dot is an overlap point where the two curves cross, and the dots are all the computer ever sees
alias.zoomTitle: Zoomed to x = 0 … ⅛ — watch {{trueF}} thread through the same overlap points that {{other}} passes through
alias.foldTitle: The folding map — where every true frequency ends up
alias.foldNote: Frequencies fold back and forth like an accordion: up to Nyquist they map to themselves, from 32 to 64 they come back mirrored, past 64 the pattern repeats. The marker is the slider's current position.
alias.whyNote: Why this matters. Between the dots the two curves disagree completely, but sampling never looks between the dots, so no algorithm can recover which wave was real: the evidence is destroyed at the moment of sampling, not by the FFT. That has a physical picture — film a wheel spinning 60 times a second with a 64-frames-per-second camera and it appears to roll slowly backwards, which is why helicopter rotors do impossible things on video. It also has an engineering consequence: since no computation can undo aliasing, real systems prevent it before sampling, with an analog filter that deletes everything above Nyquist. That is why 44.1 kHz audio can only represent tones up to about 22 kHz, and why every analog-to-digital converter ships with an anti-aliasing filter in front of it.
